title: Dress Pork Carcasses and Perform Post-slaughter Procedures for Pork Carcasses

lessons.title: Preparing the carcass: scald to clean skin
lessons.html:
Dressing a pork carcass

Dressing means turning a bled pig into a clean carcass ready for sale. Most pork is dressed with the skin on, so the skin must be clean and free of hair. This lesson covers the practical steps in the dirty area.

Step by step

  1. Check the pig is dead and well bled before it goes to the scald tank. Never scald a pig that shows signs of life.
  2. Scald in the tank or tunnel for the time and temperature your plant sets. Turn the carcass if needed so all of it is under water.
  3. Test the scald. Pull a few hairs from the back and the leg. If they come out easily, the scald is right. Report if they do not.
  4. De-hair in the de-hairing machine. Never reach in while it runs.
  5. Gambrel: open the tendons of the hind legs carefully and insert the gambrel (hanging bar), then hoist onto the rail.
  6. Singe evenly with the furnace or hand burner to remove fine hair.
  7. Scrape and shave from top to bottom: back, belly, legs, head, ears, eyelids and feet. Remove toenails (claws) as your plant requires.
  8. Wash the carcass with clean water before it enters the clean area.

Check your work

Look forAction
Hair left in folds and earsShave again
Black burnt skinScrape off
Dung or mud on skinTrim with a sterile knife, do not just wash
Torn skin or broken legReport to supervisor

Sterilise your knife between carcasses and whenever it touches something dirty.

lessons.title: Evisceration and splitting in the clean area
lessons.html:
Before you start

Change to clean-area clothing, wash hands and boots, and make sure your knives are sharp and sterilised. Keep a second knife in the sterilizer so you can swap.

Step by step

  1. Bung: cut around the anus, free it and tie it or cover it with a plastic bag so no dung can leak.
  2. Open the belly: make a small cut between the hind legs. Put two fingers inside to lift the skin away from the guts, or use the knife handle to protect them. Cut down the belly line to the breastbone, with the blade pointing outwards.
  3. Split the breastbone with a knife or brisket saw.
  4. Remove the rough offal (stomach and intestines) in one piece. Do not cut or tear the guts. Place it in the correct tray or on the offal table, matched to the carcass.
  5. Remove the pluck (tongue, throat, heart, lungs and liver) together and hang it on the pluck hook with the carcass number.
  6. Present for inspection: the carcass, head and organs go to the meat inspector together. Do not remove any part or lymph node the inspector needs.
  7. Split the carcass down the middle of the backbone with the splitting saw if you are trained and authorised.
  8. Remove the kidneys, leaf fat and spinal cord as your plant procedure says, after inspection if required.

If something goes wrong

  • Gut cut or dung on carcass: stop, tell the supervisor and have the area trimmed.
  • Carcass touches the floor: report it.
  • You see abscesses, lumps, cysts or unusual colours: tell the meat inspector. Do not cut them out yourself.

Work at a steady pace. Rushing causes gut cuts and knife injuries.

lessons.title: Post-slaughter procedures
lessons.html:
After inspection

The meat inspector decides on each carcass. You must follow the decision.

  • Passed: the carcass is marked with the approved stamp and continues.
  • Detained: moved to the detain rail for further examination. Do not touch it without permission.
  • Condemned (whole or part): put into the marked condemned bin or area, kept separate and destroyed as required.

Final trimming and washing

  1. Trim off bruises, blood clots, the sticking wound area and any small contamination with a sterile knife.
  2. Wash the sides with clean water, top to bottom, to remove bone dust and blood. Do not use the hose on contamination; trim it.

Weighing, classification and marking

Each carcass is weighed and recorded against its number and the farmer's details. Pork carcasses are classified according to the national classification system, and roller marks or labels are applied by trained, authorised staff. Check that the number, mass and owner on the kill sheet are correct.

Chilling

  • Move carcasses into the chiller promptly.
  • Hang them with space between so they do not touch each other, walls or floor.
  • Keep the doors closed. Record chiller temperatures as your plant procedure says.
  • Report a warm chiller or broken door seal at once.

Offal and by-products

Edible offal (liver, heart, kidneys, cleaned intestines if sold) is washed, chilled and kept separate from inedible material. Inedible waste goes to the correct bins for rendering or disposal.

Key points

  • Test the scald by pulling hair, and shave hair from all folds.
  • Open the belly with the blade pointing outwards to avoid gut cuts.
  • Keep the head, organs and carcass together for the meat inspector.
  • Follow every inspection decision: passed, detained or condemned.
  • Trim contamination; do not wash it off.
  • Chill quickly and record temperatures and weights correctly.
